prerequisites.item: The customer's interface name (e.g. ps127.0) — from the diacustomers record.

SSH access (username/password) to the candidate devices: LTZ-BNG02-TIG-DAR, LTZ-BNG02-RAH-DAR, LTZ-PE1-RAH, LTZ-PE1-TIG. The customer could be homed on any of these — you don't need to know which in advance.

step.title: Find the interface and confirm it's up
step.runOn: Each of the 4 candidate devices, until you find one reporting this interface.
step.lookFor: The admin and operational status columns for the ps* line.

interpretation.case: Interface doesn't exist on any candidate device — likely wrong interface name, or the circuit was never provisioned / was deprovisioned. Verify the interface name against the customer record before going further.
The circuit is down at the BNG/PE. Skip ARP and ping entirely — a down interface has no traffic to test. Go straight to Step 4 (neighbor link check) to find WHERE the fault is.
Continue to Step 2.

step.title: Discover the customer's live IP via ARP
step.runOn: The device where the interface was found up.
step.lookFor: Any IPv4 address in the output.

interpretation.case: The interface is up at the BNG but the customer's router/CPE isn't ARPing — usually means the CPE is powered off, not cabled up, or misconfigured on its WAN side. This is NOT necessarily a network-side fault. Still go to Step 4 to rule out a physical-layer problem on the access side before pointing at the customer's equipment.
Continue to Step 3.

step.title: Ping the customer's IP(s)
step.runOn: The device where the interface was found up (pings out through it toward the customer).
step.note: Up to 5 discovered IPs are tried; the check stops at the first "problematic" one.
step.lookFor: Packet loss % and average round-trip latency (ms).

interpretation.case: Marked "problematic" — customer is up but experiencing issues. Go to Step 4: this is usually explained by a physical-layer problem (flapping port, low optical power) on the access/metro leg, but can also be upstream congestion if Step 4 comes back clean.
Interface and ARP are up but the customer host is completely unreachable — check CPE power and whether the customer's router itself has failed, in addition to Step 4's link check.

Ping is healthy. Combine with Step 4's link check for a full "Customer is healthy" verdict — a clean ping with a flapping/low-power port is still worth flagging as at-risk even though the code labels it healthy.

step.title: Check the physical link on the access/metro neighbor
step.description: Run in every branch above (down, no-ARP, ping-issue, and healthy) — it explains WHERE in the chain a fault sits, or confirms the physical layer is clean when everything else looks fine.

subStep.command: show l2circuit connections interface {base}.0 | match Neighbor

interpretation.case: The l2circuit itself has no neighbor recorded — likely a config problem on the pseudowire (missing/wrong neighbor statement), not a physical fault. Escalate as a config issue rather than a field/cable issue.

subStep.runOn: The neighbor device found in 4a (SSH directly to its IP).
subStep.lookFor: A ge-*/xe-* physical port whose description references this circuit.

interpretation.case: The neighbor doesn't have a port tagged for this circuit — description/provisioning mismatch between the BNG's l2circuit config and the access switch's interface description. Treat as a provisioning/config issue.

subStep.lookFor: "Last flapped" timestamp and how long ago.
subStep.interpretation: A very recent or frequently-recurring flap timestamp lines up with intermittent packet loss / high latency from Step 3 — points to an unstable physical connection (loose patch cable, failing SFP, intermittent fiber fault) rather than a congestion issue.

subStep.command: show interface diagnostics optics {customerPort} | match power | except off
subStep.interpretation: Very low or missing receive power (well below the optic's normal operating range, or reported as an alarm/warning threshold breach) typically means a fiber problem: a bend, a dirty/damaged connector, excessive attenuation, or a degrading SFP transceiver. Power within the optic's normal range with an otherwise-clean interface points away from the physical layer and toward something upstream (congestion, core issue) or on the customer's own equipment.
Confirms which class of physical fault is even possible (optics diagnostics only matter on fiber ports).

row.symptom: Interface down + no neighbor found in 4a

symptomToCauseSummary.row: Likely l2circuit/pseudowire config issue, not a cable fault.

row.symptom: Interface down + neighbor/port found + recent flap + low optical power

symptomToCauseSummary.row: Physical fault (fiber cut, dirty connector, failing SFP) — dispatch field/access team.

row.symptom: Interface up, no ARP, port healthy in Step 4

symptomToCauseSummary.row: Customer-side issue — CPE likely powered off or misconfigured; ask customer to check equipment.

row.symptom: Ping problematic + flaps/low power on Step 4

symptomToCauseSummary.row: Physical-layer cause of the packet loss/latency.
Not a physical-layer problem — investigate upstream congestion, policer/rate-limit sizing, or core routing.
Customer is genuinely fine at the network layer; any complaint likely lives past their router (LAN/application-level).

prerequisites.item: The customer's interface name — from l3vpncustomerinfos.
The customer's routing-instance (route_instance), pulled from the DB record — needed to ping inside the correct VRF.
SSH access to the 2 candidate PE devices: LTZ-PE1-RAH, LTZ-PE1-TIG.

procedure.description: Identical shape to DIA's procedure (interface check → ARP → ping → neighbor link check), with two differences called out below. Everything else — interpretation of down/flap/optics results, the symptomToCauseSummary — applies the same way, so it isn't repeated here.
procedure.difference: Uses a stricter MAC-anchored match (only lines that look like a real ARP table row are accepted). If ARP output exists but nothing is captured, double check the interface is really in the expected routing-instance rather than assuming the customer has no IP.

difference.interpretation: If route_instance is missing/null in the DB record, the ping falls back to the global routing table — this can produce a false "unreachable" result for a VRF-only customer IP that isn't routed globally. If you get 100% loss on an L3VPN customer, confirm route_instance was actually populated before concluding the customer is down.

prerequisites.item: The customer's interface name — from iptcustomerinfos.
SSH access to the 3 candidate devices: LTZ-PE1-RAH, LTZ-PE1-TIG, LTZ-P1-DAR.
Knowledge that IPT customers peer BGP with the PE — this diagnosis checks the routing session, not raw reachability.

step.title: Find the interface and confirm it's up

interpretation.case: Skip everything below — go straight to the neighbor link check (Step 5, same as DIA Step 4).
Continue to Step 2.

step.title: Discover the customer's IP via ARP
step.lookFor: Only the FIRST IP found is used for the BGP checks below (not all of them, unlike DIA/L3VPN).

interpretation.case: Interface up but no ARP entry — same customer-CPE-not-connected reasoning as DIA. Go to the neighbor link check (Step 5) and stop.

step.title: Check the BGP session state
step.lookFor: The peer's AS number (2nd whitespace-delimited field) and implicitly whether a row exists at all.

case.result: no matching row / no ASN parsed

interpretation.case: No BGP session for this peer IP. The interface and ARP are fine, but routing was never established — check the customer's router BGP config (wrong peer-IP, wrong local ASN, missing neighbor statement, or an auth/MD5 mismatch) before assuming a network fault. Still worth a quick pass through Step 5 to rule out a flapping link causing the session to never stabilize.

case.result: ASN parsed, but you separately confirm state is not Established (Active/Connect/Idle)

interpretation.case: Session is attempting but not up — commonly a TCP-reachability problem (ACL, firewall, physical link) rather than a config typo. Step 5's link check is more likely to explain this than a pure config review.
Continue to Step 4.

step.title: Check routes actually received from the customer
step.lookFor: Any CIDR prefixes in the output.

case.result: zero routes despite an Established session

interpretation.case: The session is up but the customer isn't advertising anything — this is a customer-side routing config issue (nothing in their route-map/network statement), not a network-side fault. Session-established-with-no-routes is easy to mistake for "healthy" if you only check Step 3.
Customer is genuinely healthy — BGP up and actively advertising.

step.title: Check the physical link on the access/metro neighbor
step.description: Same sub-steps as DIA Step 4 (l2circuit neighbor → port → flaps → optics → media) — see that service's symptomToCauseSummary for interpretation; it applies unchanged here.

row.symptom: Interface up, ARP found, no BGP row at all

symptomToCauseSummary.row: Customer router-side BGP config problem (peer IP/ASN/auth) — verify with the customer before dispatching a technician.

row.symptom: Interface up, ARP found, BGP session flapping or stuck in Active/Connect/Idle

symptomToCauseSummary.row: Check Step 5's link health first — a flapping physical link commonly prevents BGP from staying Established.
Customer-side routing/advertisement issue, not a network fault — session is fine, their announcement isn't.

prerequisites.item: The customer's IP address (not an interface name — FTTH diagnosis has no Junos interface concept).
No SSH/device access needed — this check runs entirely from the application server.

step.title: Check subscription/expiry status first
step.description: Pulled from the ftthcustomers DB record, before any network probe.
step.lookFor: topUpExpiry date relative to now, and isFreeCustomer.

interpretation.case: Even if the ping in Step 2 succeeds or fails, an expired non-free subscription is the first thing to rule out — a "no_service" result for an expired customer is expected behavior (their access may be intentionally restricted), not a fault to troubleshoot.
Proceed to Step 2 as a genuine connectivity check.

step.title: Ping the customer IP directly
step.runOn: The application server itself — not any network device.
step.lookFor: Packet loss % (only 3 probes, so this is a coarse check, not a stability measurement like DIA's 20-count ping).

interpretation.case: Reported as "no_service". Because there's no device-level check in this flow (no interface status, no ONT/OLT visibility), 100% loss here does NOT distinguish between: expired subscription (already ruled out in Step 1), ONT/router powered off, a fiber fault on the GPON access network, or an OLT-side problem. If Step 1 showed an active subscription, this needs escalation to whatever tooling covers the GPON/OLT layer — this diagnosis stops at "unreachable", it can't see further into the access network.

Reported as "active" / "Customer is up with active service" — no latency/jitter threshold is applied (unlike DIA's >25ms rule), so even a poor-but-not-fully-dead connection is reported simply as active. If the customer is complaining about slowness with a non-100%-loss result here, this tool won't surface it — you'll need a manual ping with a higher count/duration, or Zabbix/OLT-side data, to see degradation.

symptomToCauseSummary.row: Expected — access intentionally restricted, not a technical fault.
Genuine outage — ONT/router power, fiber fault, or OLT-side issue; escalate to GPON/access team since this tool has no visibility past "unreachable".

row.symptom: Active subscription + partial/no loss but customer reports slowness

symptomToCauseSummary.row: This diagnosis won't detect it (no latency threshold) — investigate manually via extended ping, Zabbix, or OLT statistics.
